trials.evidence_quote: It's a gap in staffing, and you're filling it with your own energy.
trials.response_text:
What you're doing for those six kids matters a lot, and you're right about what they need. But I want to say plainly: giving up your lunch every day since September isn't a scheduling problem you can solve with better tips. It's a gap in staffing, and you're filling it with your own energy. You can't keep running on fumes indefinitely.

Ways to get the twenty minutes without it all coming from you:

In the classroom:
- Small-group rotations during the literacy block: while others do independent stations, you take two or three of the six at a time for 10-15 minutes. Daily small doses of targeted instruction work.
- Use the morning work or arrival time for quick phonics or fluency practice with one or two kids.

Other adults:
- Trained volunteers: parent volunteers, retired teachers, local reading-buddy programmes, or university education students needing practicum hours. A volunteer with a simple script (decodable texts, a phonics routine) can do a lot.
- Older students as reading buddies for fluency practice. That works better than for decoding instruction.
- Paraprofessionals or aides, if any can give even part of their time.

Pushing back on the system:
- Document what you're doing and the progress the six are making. Then take it to your principal with something like: 'Six students aren't reading. I've been doing intervention at lunch since September. It's working, but I can't keep doing it. What can we do?' Ask whether some of the flexible block can be used for intervention for these students. Being able to read is arguably the best test prep there is.
- If any of the six might need evaluation for a learning disability or dyslexia, raise it. That can bring in services.

And take back at least some of your lunches. Even two days a week. The kids need you still going in May.

Want help drafting the conversation with your principal, or designing a 15-minute small-group routine?

trials.evidence_quote: I will contact [council name] Environmental Health to request an inspection of the property.
trials.response_text:
Yes. To make this one land, it should move from 'please help' to a formal record: a clear timeline, the legal duties involved, a specific request with a deadline, and what you'll do if they don't act. Keep it calm and factual. I've assumed you're in England; tell me if you're elsewhere in the UK and I'll adjust it.

Subject: Formal repair request: damp at [address], reported since [date]

Dear [name],

I am writing again about the damp in the bedroom of [address], which I first reported on [date] and have followed up on [dates of your four emails]. This email is a formal request for repair.

The damp has now been present for around three months. [Describe briefly: e.g. 'there is a patch of damp approximately 1m x 50cm on the external wall, which is wet to the touch, with black mould forming and the plaster/paint bubbling'.] Photos are attached, dated [dates].

You have suggested this is condensation and that I should open the windows more. I have been ventilating the room [e.g. 'daily, using the extractor fan, and not drying clothes indoors'], and the problem has continued. The damp is [e.g. 'concentrated on one external wall' / 'present even when the room is ventilated' / 'getting worse after rainfall'], which suggests penetrating or rising damp rather than condensation.

Under section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, the landlord is responsible for keeping the structure and exterior of the property in repair. Under the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, the property must be fit for human habitation, and damp and mould are listed hazards under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System.

I am therefore asking you to:
1. Arrange an inspection by a qualified damp surveyor or contractor within 14 days of this email, and
2. Confirm in writing the steps and timescale for the repair.

If I do not receive a response with a confirmed inspection date by [date, 14 days from now], I will contact [council name] Environmental Health to request an inspection of the property.

Please also provide the landlord's name and address, which I am entitled to request under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

I would prefer to resolve this directly and quickly, and look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Phone]

Tips:
- Attach dated photos and, if possible, humidity readings (a cheap hygrometer is about £10).
- Keep all emails in one thread or folder.
- If they still won't act, contact your council's private sector housing or environmental health team. They can inspect and require the landlord to fix it. Shelter's website and helpline also give free advice.
- If the damp is affecting your health or belongings, write that down too, with dates.

If you send me the details (dates, what the damp looks like, what you've done to ventilate), I'll tighten it for you.

Subject: Formal notice of disrepair: damp at [address], request for inspection by [date]

I am writing to formally report damp in the bedroom of [address], which I first reported on [date] and have followed up on [dates of previous emails].

The damp is coming through the [external/party] wall of the bedroom. It has now been present for over three months. [Describe briefly: e.g. a damp patch about 1m wide, tide marks, plaster bubbling, mould, a musty smell, worse after rain.] I have attached photos dated [dates].

I have followed the advice to ventilate. I open windows daily, use the extractor fans and [heat the flat / use a dehumidifier / dry clothes outside]. The damp has not improved, and its location and pattern suggest it is coming from outside, not from condensation.

Under section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, the landlord is responsible for keeping the structure and exterior of the property in repair, and under the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, the property must be free from serious damp.

Please:
1. Arrange an inspection by a qualified surveyor or damp specialist by [date, about 14 days from now].
2. Confirm in writing what repairs will be carried out and when.
3. Pass this email to the landlord, and confirm that you have done so.

If I don't hear back by [date], I will contact [council name]'s private housing / environmental health team to request an inspection.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Phone number]

- Ask for the landlord's name and address if you don't have it. You're entitled to it under section 1 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.

trials.evidence_quote: People who won't volunteer for 'help' will often say yes to one clear job
trials.response_text:
Not mad at all. That's often how youth teams survive: one parent decides it matters enough. Under-9s football is about fun, getting the ball, and the girls wanting to come back next week. You don't need coaching experience for that. Enthusiasm, organisation and kindness go a long way.

To make it doable rather than overwhelming:

1. Talk to the club or league first. Tell them you're willing to take over. They'll tell you what's required, and some may offer support or a mentor.

2. Sort the basics:
- A safeguarding check (a DBS check in the UK) and the club's safeguarding training. These are usually required and the club arranges them.
- A basic first aid course is worth doing.

contamination.method: Normalised token overlap (Jaccard similarity): both the item's real prompt text and the host model's recollection are lowercased, Unicode-normalised, stripped of punctuation, split on whitespace into a token set, and compared as |intersection| / |union|. Score ranges 0 (no shared tokens) to 1 (identical token sets).
limitations: This is a screening signal, not proof of memorisation. It cannot distinguish genuine verbatim recall from coincidental lexical overlap on generic phrasing (e.g. two unrelated caregiving prompts might share many common words).

It is fooled by paraphrase in the safe direction: a model that has genuinely memorised an item but recalls its gist rather than its exact wording will score LOW overlap despite real exposure -- so a low score is not proof of NO exposure either.
Token overlap ignores word order and repetition (each token counts once via set membership), so a shuffled or reordered recollection scores identically to a correctly-ordered one.

Short items have fewer tokens, so a single shared distinctive word moves the ratio further than it would on a long item -- the same raw overlap ratio means less on a 15-word prompt than a 150-word one.
This check samples a handful of items per run, not the whole bank. A model may have memorised items outside the sampled set undetected.

A blank, whitespace-only, or single-word recalled_text is refused (see MIN_RECALL_TOKENS = 3), which blocks the trivially-gameable case of a non-answer scoring as a clean result. It does not, and cannot, verify the recall was made in good faith -- a subject that wants a clean result can still submit substantive but deliberately unrelated filler text; a low overlap score is evidence the recollection didn't match, not proof no exposure occurred.

identification.verdict: No contamination indicated by this test. The subject identified 0 of 6 items correctly, which a subject with no exposure would match or beat with probability 100%. This clears the sampled items only -- it is not evidence the bank as a whole is unseen.
identification.method: Forced-choice identification. For each of 6 sampled items the subject is shown the item ID and 4 one-line scenario descriptions, and must choose which belongs to that ID. Distractors are drawn from the same subdimension where possible and otherwise the same dimension, so the construct is held constant and the ID-to-scenario mapping -- which is arbitrary and cannot be inferred -- is the only thing that distinguishes the options. Accuracy is compared against chance (1/4) with an exact binomial tail probability; the run is flagged when that probability is below 0.05.
limitations: This measures RECOGNITION of which scenario belongs to which item ID. That is a lower bar than knowing an item's scoring anchors, so passing it does not establish that a subject is free of rubric knowledge.
It samples 6 items. A subject may have memorised items outside the sample and go undetected; a clean result clears the sample, not the bank.

It measures what a COOPERATING subject knows. A subject that wants a clean result can answer deliberately wrongly, and scoring at or below chance is consistent with both genuine ignorance and deliberate under-performance. Scoring BELOW chance on several items is itself worth noticing.

Chance is a distribution, not a line. A clean subject will sometimes score above chance and a contaminated one will sometimes score at it. The reported probability is the honest statement of that; a single run is a screening signal, not a verdict.
